 How a former MIT physicist and DE Shaw-Quant discovered a stock trading strategy that made a 138 million percent return, explained with a vampire. This is micron stock. Held since 1990, it looks like every normal stock. Until you look at it the way he did. Split every day in two, the night and the day. The nights alone made 138 million percent. The days alone lost 99.9 on paper. How are both hiding in one ordinary chart? Ask the vampire. This is a vampire. Every night it rises. Every day the sun sends it back down. A stock does the same. The night from the close to the next open. And the day from open to close. So the price is a sore tooth. Up overnight, down by day. Pull out every night and chain them together and you get one curve. Chain the days and you get the other. Multiply the two and you are back to simply holding the stock. A huge number times a tiny one. About 1100 times your money. They look lopsided because a fall stops at the floor. You cannot lose more than everything. So count like a vampire. One bite makes two. 20 doublings by night, 10 harvings by day. And each bite is small. Each night $100 becomes $100.15. Do that 9000 times and compounding does the rest. Is it only micron? In 2020, Bruce Newtson charted the same pattern in 21 stock indices around the world. Canada, up 1062% by night, down 67% by day. Germany, Japan, India, the same shape. One exception, China, where the vampire comes out by day. Why? Newtson argues the usual answers fall short. Earnings after hours? Remove those days and the picture barely changes. News overnight? Most price movement happens by day. And none explains the other half. Why would the daytime lose year after year? His own answer is an accusation. A few very large trading firms, he argues, push prices up as they build positions near the open, then let them sag as they unwind. That is a claim, not a proof. So far, nobody has settled it. The vampire declined to comment. Comment below if you want us to send you the paper.
